source_text: THESIS I. DURANDUS Vir inter Veteres Scholasticos celebris, censuit & docuit Deum cum causis secundis concurrere remote & mediate solum: nempe quia rebus omnibus propriam naturam & essentiam dedit, & facultatem agendi contulit, ac utramque Virtute sua continuo conservat: ea lege, ut creaturae singulae Virtute semel a Deo indita, & perpetuo conservata, proprios motus deinceps obeant; absque eo quod Deus earum actus & effectus immediate & per se attingat: Unde sequitur Deum actuum creaturae causam tantum remotam esse, solam vero creaturam causam proximam & immediatam.
english: Durandus, a well-known figure among the older scholastics, held and taught that God concurs with secondary causes only remotely and mediately.

On his account God gave everything its own nature and essence, bestowed the power to act, and keeps both in being by his continual power. He did so on the understanding that each creature, by the power God once placed in it and always sustains, then carries out its own motions, without God touching its acts and effects directly and of himself. It follows that God is only the remote cause of what creatures do, and the creature alone is the proximate and immediate cause.

source_text: II. Inter recentiores vero Ludovicus quidam a Dola ex ordine Capucinorum, cujus liber cum multis Doctorum approbationibus in lucem editus est, ad illam Durandi sententiam accedit. Dicit enim, Deum cum homine in agendo concurrere nihil aliud esse quam Vel liberum arbitrium creare, ut in actibus naturalibus, Vel dare in supernaturalibus potentiam, seu habitum agendi, per quam ipsa Voluntas totum faciat in omni actu supernaturali, absque ullo alio Dei concursu immediato actionem actu promovente. Prout hujus Viri Verba referuntur a Samuele Retorforti Theologiae Professore in Academia Andreapolitana Disputatione Scholastica de divina providentia cap. 25.
english: Among more recent writers, a certain Louis of Dole, of the Capuchin order, whose book appeared with many approvals from theologians, comes over to Durandus's view.

He says that God's concurring with man in action amounts to nothing more than creating free choice, in natural acts, or, in supernatural acts, giving a power or habit of acting by which the will itself does the entire work in every supernatural act, without any further immediate concurrence of God actually advancing the action. His words are reported in this form by Samuel Rutherford, professor of theology at the University of St Andrews, in his Scholastic Disputation on Divine Providence, chapter 25.

source_text: III. Porro juxta hos Doctores nulla est difficultas in conciliando divino concursu cum libertate actuum humanorum, quandoquidem Deus ad illos immediate non concurrit, sed mediate tantum per liberum arbitrium quod semel creavit & perpetuo conservat.
english: For these teachers, then, reconciling God's concurrence with the freedom of human acts poses no problem at all.
God does not concur in those acts immediately, but only mediately, through the free choice he created once and keeps in being without interruption.

source_text: IV. Verum ista opinio communiter in Schola Romana rejicitur. Paucissimis enim exceptis, consentiunt Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae tum Veteres tum recentiores, Deum ita cooperari causis secundis ut nulla sit actio causae secundae quae proxime non procedat a Deo sicut & a causa secunda, & nullam actionem posse a creatura exerceri, nisi Deus cum creatura conferat Esse illi actioni, & quidem per se & immediate.
english: The Roman School, however, generally rejects this view. With very few exceptions, the teachers of the Roman Church, old and recent alike, agree that God cooperates with secondary causes in such a way that every action of a secondary cause comes proximately from God as well as from that cause.
No action can be performed by a creature unless God, together with the creature, gives that action its being, and does so of himself and directly.

source_text: V. Illud autem colligunt ex quibusdam Scripturae locis. Praecipuus ille est qui habetur Act. 17. 28. In ipso vivimus & movemur & sumus. Quum enim dicit Apostolus nos in Deo, id est, per illum & esse & vivere, satis docet Deum esse qui & naturam & facultates omnes nobis initio dedit & jugiter conservat; adeoque quum addit nos quoque in Deo moveri, plane docere videtur omnes nostros motus atque actiones sicut naturam ipsam, immediate a Deo procedere, & Virtute illius fieri.
english: They draw this from certain passages of Scripture, chiefly Acts 17:28: 'In him we live and move and have our being.'

When the Apostle says that we exist and live in God, that is, through him, he makes it clear enough that God gave us our nature and all our powers at the start and constantly sustains them. And when he adds that we also move in God, he appears to teach outright that all our movements and actions, like our nature itself, come directly from God and are carried out by his power.

source_text: VI. Huc etiam referunt quod dicit Christus Joan. 5. 17. Pater meus usque modo operatur & ego operor. Etenim jugis illa operatio quae ibi Deo tribuitur, commodius exponi non potest quam de influxu continuo quo Deus ad omnes rerum creatarum actiones concurrit easque cum illis producit: praesertim cum manifestum sit Christum illic intelligere operationem similem ejus quam modo in sanatione claudi exercuerat.
english: They also cite Christ's words in John 5:17: 'My Father is working until now, and I am working.'

The unceasing work ascribed to God there, they argue, is best explained as the continual influence by which God concurs in every action of created things and produces those actions together with them. This is all the more so because Christ clearly has in mind a work like the one he had just done in healing the lame man.

source_text: VII. Idem praeterea inferri posse putant ex omnibus iis locis ubi Scriptura Deo singulariter tribuit ea quae quotidie fiunt in natura per causas secundas. Ut quum Psalm. 104. dicitur Deus rigare montes de superioribus suis, producere foenum jumentis & herbam quae homini serviat. Et Psalm. 135. Educere nubes ab extremo terrae, fulgura in viam facere, Et producere Ventos de thesauris suis. Et in Novo Testamento foenum agri circumvestire, id est, ornare floribus, Et Unicuique seminum dare proprium corpus, Matth. 6. 30. 1 Cor. 15. 38. Nec enim videtur Scriptura his & similibus modis loquendi usura fuisse, si in ejusmodi rebus nulla singularis & immediata Dei actio interveniret: nec aliam causam haberent proximam & immediatam, quam naturam ipsam a Deo creatam.
english: They also think the same can be inferred from every passage in which Scripture assigns to God, one by one, the things that happen daily in nature through secondary causes.

So in Psalm 104 God is said to water the mountains from his upper rooms and to make grass grow for the cattle and plants to serve mankind. In Psalm 135 he brings up clouds from the ends of the earth, makes lightning for the rain, and brings the winds out of his storehouses. In the New Testament he clothes the grass of the field, that is, decks it with flowers, and gives each kind of seed its own body (Matthew 6:30; 1 Corinthians 15:38).

Scripture would hardly have spoken this way, they argue, if no particular and immediate act of God were involved in such things and they had no proximate and immediate cause other than nature itself as God created it.

source_text: VIII. Illis vero Scripturae sacrae testimoniis addunt etiam argumentum a ratione naturali petitum, sic enim ratiocinantur. Nullae substantiae creatae in rerum natura permanere possunt, nisi Deus illas immediate influxu suo conservet; multo magis ergo simili influxu egent substantiarum motus & actiones: quomodo enim verum esse posset accidentia minus a Deo pendere ad sui conservationem quam ipsas substantias? Cum vero id quod ad conservationem rei est necessarium, majori cum ratione necessarium sit ad primam ejusdem rei productionem, inde consequens est ut nihil omnino a causis secundis valeat produci, nisi simul actualis immediatusque influxus causae primae interveniat.
english: To these scriptural testimonies they add an argument from natural reason, which runs as follows. No created substance can continue to exist unless God keeps it in being by his immediate influence. Much more, then, do the motions and actions of substances need such influence, for how could accidents depend less on God for their preservation than substances do?

Moreover, whatever a thing needs in order to be kept in being, it needs all the more in order to be produced in the first place. It follows that secondary causes can produce nothing whatever unless an actual and immediate influence of the first cause is present at the same time.

source_text: IX. Ex his & similibus, communi jam fere consensu, concludunt Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae Deum cum causis omnibus secundis, sive necessariis, sive liberis, aut contingentibus, ad singulos earum actus concurrere & cooperari, & quidem proxime & immediate. Attamen quum quaeritur quae sit illa causae primae cum causa secunda cooperatio, & qua in re consistat, magna reperitur inter Doctores Scholasticos sententiarum varietas.
english: From these and like arguments the teachers of the Roman Church now conclude, almost unanimously, that God concurs and cooperates with every secondary cause, necessary, free or contingent, in each of its acts, and does so proximately and immediately.
But when one asks what this cooperation of the first cause with the secondary cause is and what it consists in, the scholastic teachers turn out to hold widely different views.

source_text: X. Thomas & plerique illius sequaces, quales praecipue sunt Dominicani, docent ad divinum concursum explicandum, non satis esse si dicamus simpliciter, Deum influere in actus & effecta varia causarum secundarum, illisque tribuere & conservare suum esse, sicut ipsas causas secundas, & earum Virtutes creavit & conservat: Sed praeterea requiri contendunt, ut Deus ipsas causas secundas praemoveat & applicet ad opus, absque quo nihil illae prorsus acturae forent. Hoc enim exigere dependentiam causarum secundarum a Deo, ut a primo movente. Quippe ex eorum mente Deus propterea dicitur primum movens, quia ipse omnes alias causas antecedenter movet & applicat ad operationes suas, adeoque prius natura, etsi non tempore, effectus omnes causarum secundarum producit. Ut loquitur Estius in 2. Sententia ad distinct. 24. paragr. 14.
english: Thomas and most of his followers, chiefly the Dominicans, teach that to explain God's concurrence it is not enough to say simply that God flows into the various acts and effects of secondary causes and gives them and keeps them in being, as he created and keeps in being the secondary causes themselves and their powers.

They insist that something more is needed: God must premove the secondary causes and apply them to their work, without which they would do nothing whatever. This, they say, is what the dependence of secondary causes on God as first mover requires.

On their view God is called the first mover precisely because he moves all other causes beforehand and applies them to their operations, and so produces all the effects of secondary causes first in the order of nature, though not of time. So Estius puts it on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 24, paragraph 14.

source_text: XI. Quae videtur esse Doctrina Catechismi ipsius Romani Tridentini Concilii jussu in lucem editi, cujus haec Verba sunt in explicatione Symboli ad primum articulum sub finem. Non solum Deus Universa quae sunt providentia sua tuetur atque administrat, Verum etiam quae moventur & agunt aliquid, intima Virtute ad motum atque actionem ita impellit; ut quamvis causarum secundarum efficientiam non impediat, praeveniat tamen: cum ejus occultissima vis ad singula pertineat, & quemadmodum sapiens testatur, Attingat a fine usque ad finem fortiter, &c.
english: This appears to be the teaching of the Roman Catechism itself, published by order of the Council of Trent. Toward the end of its explanation of the first article of the Creed it says:

'God not only protects and governs by his providence everything that exists. He also so drives the things that move and act, by an inward power, to their motion and action that, while he does not hinder the efficiency of secondary causes, he goes before it, since his most hidden power reaches to every single thing and, as the wise man testifies, "reaches mightily from one end to the other", and so on.'

source_text: XII. Igitur illi volunt Deum ciere atque applicare causam secundam ad agendum, & ratione ac natura prius quam creatura operetur, illam a Deo moveri efficaciter in singulis ejus actionibus; Deumque esse qui agit & facit ut creatura agat & faciat quicquid illa facit & agit: ita ut sine hac Dei praemotione nihil omnino possit agere creatura, & data hac praemotione impossibile sit in sensu composito, causam secundam non illud agere & facere, ad quod a prima causa praemovetur.
english: They hold, therefore, that God rouses and applies the secondary cause to act, and that before the creature works, in the order of reason and nature, God effectively moves it in each of its actions. It is God who acts and brings it about that the creature acts and does whatever it does.

Without this premotion from God the creature can do nothing at all; and once the premotion is given, it is impossible, in the composite sense, for the secondary cause not to do and make what the first cause premoves it to.

source_text: XIII. Cum vero juxta eorum sententiam, divina ista praemotio locum habeat non minus in agentibus liberis quam in necessariis, inde oritur non parva difficultas, quomodo illud cum creaturarum libertate constare possit. Si enim Voluntas nostra nihil agere potest, nisi a Deo prius moveatur, atque ad opus applicetur, quomodo censeri poterit domina sui actus, & indifferens esse ad agendum, vel non agendum; quandoquidem non habet in sua potestate divinam illam motionem & applicationem, quae ad singulos ejus actus praerequiritur? Et rursus quum Deus Voluntatem movet & applicat ad opus, qui possit dici Voluntas libere operari, cum non possit non operari, & motioni divinae resistere?
english: Since on their view this divine premotion applies to free agents no less than to necessary ones, a considerable difficulty arises: how can it be reconciled with the freedom of creatures?

If our will can do nothing unless God first moves it and applies it to its work, how can it be considered mistress of its own act and indifferent to acting or not acting, when the divine motion and application required beforehand for each of its acts is not in its power? And again, when God moves the will and applies it to its work, how can the will be said to act freely, when it can neither refrain from acting nor resist the divine motion?

source_text: XIV. Bellarminus ut difficultatem illam solvat, dicit influxum, seu Virtutem Dei, qua Voluntas movetur & applicatur ad opus, recipi in causis secundis secundum illarum dispositionem. Illa vero dispositio secundum quam recipitur in Voluntate motus Dei, Bellarmino nihil aliud est quam negativa quaedam determinatio praecedens tum influxum Dei, tum actum elicitum Voluntatis. Nimirum illa ex ejus sensu, in eo consistit quod Voluntas sinat se moveri ab objecto per rationem ipsi proposito, vel ab eo se moveri non sinat. Quam determinationem dicit esse negativam, quia non consistit in actu positivo, sed in negatione actus; cum tamen Voluntas non minus sit libera ut agat, quam ut non agat. Unde fieri putat ut Voluntas sit vere libera, & ipsa se determinet, tametsi Deus illam moveat & applicet ad opus, quia, scilicet, ipsa Dei motio in ejus potestate est. Nam, inquit, si se moveri sinat ab objecto proposito, Deus eam applicat & movet ad actum eliciendum: si non sinat, Deus eam non applicat neque movet: ad hoc, scilicet, Deus se libere obligavit, quando liberam Voluntatem creavit. De Liber. Arbitr. lib. 4. cap. 16.
english: To resolve that difficulty Bellarmine says that God's influence or power, by which the will is moved and applied to its work, is received in secondary causes according to their disposition.

For Bellarmine the disposition according to which God's motion is received in the will is simply a kind of negative determination that comes before both God's influence and the will's elicited act. In his sense it consists in the will's letting itself be moved by the object that reason sets before it, or not letting itself be moved by it. He calls the determination negative because it lies not in a positive act but in the absence of one, though the will is no less free to act than not to act.

This, he thinks, is how the will is truly free and determines itself even though God moves it and applies it to its work: God's motion itself is in the will's power. 'If it lets itself be moved by the object set before it,' he says, 'God applies it and moves it to produce the act; if it does not, God neither applies it nor moves it. God freely bound himself to this when he created a free will.' (De libero arbitrio, book 4, chapter 16.)

source_text: XV. Itaque ad argumentum, ex Bellarmini mente, dicendum est, quanquam Voluntas ad agendum egeat Dei motione praevia, & applicatione ad opus, illam tamen semper esse actus sui dominam; quia nimirum motionem illam quadantenus habet in sua potestate, qua ratione jam expositum est. Et quamvis posita Dei motione impossibile sit quin voluntas moveatur, voluntatem tamen semper in agendo liberam esse, quia fuit in ejus potestate a Deo non moveri; nempe se non disponendo per negativam illam determinationem ad motionem Dei recipiendam, quod erat penes voluntatem.
english: On Bellarmine's view, then, the answer to the objection is this. Although the will needs God's prior motion and application in order to act, it is always mistress of its act, because it has that motion in its power to some degree, in the way just explained.

Once God's motion is given, the will cannot fail to be moved; yet it is always free in acting, because it was in its power not to be moved by God, namely by not disposing itself, through that negative determination, to receive his motion. That was up to the will.

source_text: XVI. Verum ista Bellarmini solutio non placet multis eorum qui cum Thoma sentiunt, Voluntati, ut reliquis omnibus causis secundis, necessariam esse ad agendum praeviam quandam Dei motionem & applicationem. Statuunt enim Deum, absque ulla consideratione istiusmodi negativae determinationis quae in Voluntate creata praecesserit, Voluntatem pro suo arbitrio movere; neque movere simpliciter, sed ad sic, vel sic operandum efficaciter impellere: ita ut Voluntas ad hoc, & non aliud agendum, hoc volendum, illud nolendum a Deo determinetur, prius natura quam ipsa se determinet.
english: Bellarmine's solution does not satisfy many of those who hold with Thomas that the will, like every other secondary cause, needs a certain prior motion and application from God in order to act.

They maintain that God moves the will as he chooses, without any regard to a negative determination of that kind that may have preceded in the created will. He does not merely move it but efficaciously impels it to act in this way or that, so that the will is determined by God to do this and not something else, to will this and refuse that, first in the order of nature, before it determines itself.

source_text: XVII. Et haec est quae ab ipsis dicitur Praedeterminatio, quam etiam Physicam appellant, non prout Physicum, id est, naturale opponitur Supernaturali, sed prout Physicum opponitur Morali. Nimirum volunt Deum Voluntates creatas ad agendum praedeterminare, non simpliciter objectum proponendo, suadendo, alliciendo, quae sunt Causae Moralis propria; sed immediate ipsam Voluntatem movendo, & actionem veram, realem & proprie dictam in eam exercendo, quod est proprium causae quae Physica vocatur.
english: This is what they call predetermination, and they also call it physical, not in the sense in which the physical, meaning the natural, is opposed to the supernatural, but in the sense in which the physical is opposed to the moral.

They hold that God predetermines created wills to act not merely by presenting an object, urging and attracting, which is what a moral cause does, but by moving the will itself directly and exerting on it a true, real action in the proper sense, which is what belongs to a cause called physical.

source_text: XVIII. Istiusmodi vero praedeterminationem locum habere volunt non tantum in actibus bonis causarum liberarum, sed etiam in malis. Cum enim existiment eam esse causae secundae dependentiam a prima ut nihil omnino operari possit, nisi a prima moveatur, & ad agendum applicetur tanquam illius instrumentum, huic suo dogmati consentanee docent, etiam ad actus illos quibus adhaeret aliqua malitia & pravitas, Voluntatem creatam sic a Deo praemoveri & praedeterminari, ut posita Dei motione, illam hoc & illud agere necesse sit.
english: They hold that predetermination of this kind takes place not only in the good acts of free causes but in their evil acts too.

Since they think that the secondary cause depends on the first so completely that it can do nothing unless the first moves it and applies it to act as its instrument, they teach, consistently with that doctrine, that even for acts tainted with some malice and depravity the created will is premoved and predetermined by God in such a way that, once God's motion is given, it must do this or that.

source_text: XIX. Inde tamen sequi negant Deum esse peccati authorem: quoniam Deus in actu peccati non aliud efficit quam id quod in eo est positivum, adeoque bonum; ac proinde non ad aliud movet & determinat: pravitas vero & vitiositas quae tali actui adhaeret, non est aliquid positivum, quod opus habeat causa proprie efficiente, sed solum rectitudinis debitae privatio, quae ex defectu creatae Voluntatis oritur.
english: They deny, however, that it follows that God is the author of sin. In an act of sin God brings about only what is positive in it, and therefore good, and moves and determines the will to nothing beyond that.

The depravity and corruption attached to such an act is nothing positive requiring a cause that properly produces it. It is only the absence of the rightness the act ought to have, and it arises from the failure of the created will.

source_text: XX. Hanc doctrinam accurate & distincte tradit Didacus Alvares in Summa Operis de Auxiliis divinae gratiae libro secundo. Etenim in eo libro capitis septimi Lemma est, Quod Deus praevia motione Voluntati creatae inhaerente eam ad modum causae Physicae moveat, applicet, seu praedeterminet ad omnes actus suos bonos in particulari, salva ipsius libertate. Et in eo capite haec sunt illius verba, Per hanc motionem & applicationem Deus transmutat realiter Voluntatem de uno in aliud, & facit illam de Nolente Volentem. Item, Deus hac actuali motione efficaci ad modum causae Physicae, id est, vere efficienter, praedeterminat hominis Voluntatem ad liberos actus bonos, ut Voluntas a Deo mota per hujusmodi auxilium se libere & infallibiliter determinet ad actum secundum libere producendum.
english: Diego Alvarez sets out this teaching accurately and clearly in the Summa of his work De auxiliis divinae gratiae, book 2. The heading of chapter 7 there reads: 'That God, by a prior motion inhering in the created will, moves, applies, or predetermines it in the manner of a physical cause to all its good acts in particular, without prejudice to its freedom.'

In that chapter he writes: 'By this motion and application God really changes the will from one state to another and makes it willing instead of unwilling.' And again: 'By this actual, efficacious motion, in the manner of a physical cause, that is, truly as an efficient cause, God predetermines man's will to free good acts, so that the will, moved by God through help of this kind, determines itself freely and infallibly to produce its second act freely.'

source_text: XXI. Caput vero nonum hunc titulum praefert. Quod Deus praevia motione liberum arbitrium vere efficienter, sive ad modum causae Physicae, praemoveat ad actum peccati, in quantum actus, & ut ens est. Ipsum vero caput incipit his verbis, Quae dicta sunt de praedeterminatione Voluntatis ad actus bonos, extendi debent ad actum peccati, in quantum actus & ens est. Unde quicquid entitatis reperitur in quocunque actu peccati, etiamsi alias sit intrinsece malus, debet reduci in Deum, tanquam in primam causam praemoventem, & praedeterminantem actuali motione Voluntatem creatam ad talem actum, in quantum actus est, & secundum quod est ens. Postea vero ostensurus quomodo ex eo quod Deus est causa prima praemovens, & praedeterminans voluntatem creatam ad actum intrinsece malum, exempli gratia ad actum blasphemiae, aut odii in Deum, non sequitur Deum esse causam malitiae moralis quae talibus actibus inest, dicit deformitatem peccati, seu malitiam moralem non sequi intrinsece, & ex natura rei ad actum blasphemiae, vel odii Dei, secundum suam essentiam, ut actus est; neque ut est ens in genere naturae, etiam in individuo; sed ut procedit a voluntate creata deficiente; & ideo in voluntatem deficientem, & non in Deum, debere refundi malitiam moralem, & defectum peccati.
english: The heading of chapter 9 reads: 'That God, by a prior motion, truly as an efficient cause or in the manner of a physical cause, premoves free choice to the act of sin insofar as it is an act and a being.'

The chapter opens: 'What has been said about the predetermination of the will to good acts must be extended to the act of sin insofar as it is an act and a being. Hence whatever being is found in any act of sin, even one otherwise intrinsically evil, must be traced back to God as the first cause who premoves and, by an actual motion, predetermines the created will to that act insofar as it is an act and insofar as it is a being.'

Then, to show why it does not follow from God's being the first cause who premoves and predetermines the created will to an intrinsically evil act, such as blasphemy or hatred of God, that God causes the moral malice in such acts, he says this: the deformity of sin, or moral malice, does not follow intrinsically and by the nature of the case from the act of blasphemy or hatred of God in its essence as an act, nor as a being in the order of nature, even taken individually. It follows from the act as it comes from a created will that fails. The moral malice and the defect of sin must therefore be laid on the failing will, not on God.

source_text: XXII. Atque his consentanea sunt quae leguntur apud Estium loco supra citato, ubi exposita eadem sententia, & multis in illius confirmationem adductis, sic concludit, & adversus voluntatis humanae libertatem sibi objicit, Cum igitur ex dictis pateat voluntatem nostram ad actiones suas efficaciter moveri & determinari a Deo tanquam prima causa, primoque agente, movente, deliberante, & proinde ab eo praeveniri ac praedeterminari, restat explicandum quomodo cum efficaci illa motione, ac determinatione, imo praemotione ac praedeterminatione divina, consistat libertas voluntatis nostrae. Non enim videtur relinqui liberum ad utrumlibet id quod a priori causa efficaciter movetur & determinatur in alteram partem.
english: What Estius writes in the passage cited above agrees with this. Having set out the same view and brought many arguments to support it, he concludes as follows and raises against himself the objection from the freedom of the human will:

'Since, then, what has been said makes it clear that our will is efficaciously moved and determined to its actions by God as first cause, first agent, mover and deliberator, and is therefore anticipated and predetermined by him, it remains to explain how the freedom of our will is consistent with that efficacious motion and determination, indeed with divine premotion and predetermination. For what a prior cause efficaciously moves and determines to one side does not seem to be left free to go either way.'

source_text: XXIII. Ad hoc vero respondet ad rationem liberi arbitrii; hoc sufficere, ut ex praevio judicio intellectus practici, sic eligat unum oppositorum, ut tamen ex ejusdem intellectus diverso judicio possit eligere alterum; quia, scilicet, radix & fundamentum libertatis arbitrii est in intellectu, quatenus ille diversas boni rationes circa opposita potest considerare, & voluntati proponere, rationem vero liberi arbitrii non includere, ut dum agens liberum ex judicio praevio eligit, ad sic judicandum atque eligendum non moveatur ab aliqua causa superiori. Ac proinde cum motio Dei voluntatem praedeterminans non impediat quominus homo plenum atque perfectum habeat judicium rationis, & judicet aliud medium esse contingens, aliud autem cum fine ex necessitate connexum, & posset quoque ex diverso judicio aliud eligere, hoc ipso, talem motionem libertati Voluntatis nostrae nihil officere. Quippe proprium esse Voluntatis increatae ut electionem suam ab aliquo priori non habeat.
english: His answer is that for the nature of free choice it is enough that the will, on a prior judgment of the practical intellect, chooses one of two opposites in such a way that it could choose the other on a different judgment of the same intellect. The root and foundation of freedom of choice lies in the intellect, insofar as it can weigh different aspects of good in opposite options and set them before the will.

The nature of free choice does not require that a free agent, when it chooses on a prior judgment, should not be moved by some higher cause to judge and choose as it does. So, since God's motion predetermining the will does not prevent a man from having a full and complete judgment of reason, judging one means contingent and another necessarily connected with the end, and being able to choose differently on a different judgment, that motion does the freedom of our will no harm. It belongs only to the uncreated will not to receive its choice from something prior.

source_text: XXIV. Alia tamen ratione conciliare conatur Alvares Physicam illam Voluntatis humanae praedeterminationem ad actus ipsius singulos per Dei moventis impulsum, cum libera ejusdem Voluntatis electione. Postquam enim hanc sibi objectionem proposuit, si praevius ille Dei influxus in causam est necessarius, ut Voluntas operetur, sequitur quod sine illo operari non possit, & ita peribit ejus libertas, Respondet, Praevia illa motio, sive influxus immediatus in causam, non est necessarius ut Voluntas possit operari, si velit; id enim habet per propriam Virtutem, aut per habitus supernaturales; sed solum est necessarius ut actualiter operetur. Unde ex eo quod voluntas non moveatur a Deo praevia illa motione, non sequitur quod non possit velle, aut operari; sed solum infertur quod de facto non sit operatura.
english: Alvarez, however, tries another way to reconcile the physical predetermination of the human will to each of its acts by the impulse of God moving it with the will's free choice.

He sets himself this objection: 'If God's prior influence on the cause is necessary for the will to act, it follows that without it the will cannot act, and so its freedom is lost.' He replies: 'That prior motion, or immediate influence on the cause, is not needed for the will to be able to act if it wishes; it has that through its own power, or through supernatural habits. It is needed only for the will actually to act. So from the fact that God does not move the will by that prior motion, it does not follow that the will cannot will or act; it follows only that it will not in fact act.'

source_text: XXV. Ejusdem vero libri cap. 6. Responsione ad secundum argumentum, ex eo quod Deus aliquem praedeterminavit ad hoc, vel illud volendum, negat sequi quod absolute loquendo, non sit in potestate ejus aliud velle, quamvis ex suppositione divinae illius praedeterminationis, impossibile sit, in sensu composito, quod velit aliud objectum. Uno verbo distinguit inter velle & operari, & posse velle atque operari; & concedit absque influxu illo praedeterminante voluntatem nunquam operari, cum eo vero voluntatem nunquam non operari: sed pertendit, cum illo voluntatem habere potestatem non operandi, & contra absque illo voluntatem habere potestatem operandi, scilicet in sensu diviso. Nimirum ex ejus mente, cum influxu isto praedeterminante stat potentia voluntatis ad non agendum, aut aliter agendum; non stat vero actus oppositus, aut cessatio ab actu. Et vice versa, absque illo influxu manet in voluntate potentia agendi, licet absque illo nunquam in actum educatur. Inde autem colligit fieri ut omittens actum qui est in praecepto libere illum omittat, & peccet; quia per auxilium sufficiens poterat implere illud praeceptum; ex Dei autem misericordia poterat habere motionem illam ad agendum necessariam, sua vero culpa impedivit ne illi donaretur a Deo.
english: In chapter 6 of the same book, answering the second argument, he denies that because God has predetermined someone to will this or that, it is not, absolutely speaking, in his power to will something else, although on the supposition of that divine predetermination it is impossible, in the composite sense, for him to will another object.

In short, he distinguishes between willing and acting on the one hand and being able to will and act on the other. He grants that without that predetermining influence the will never acts, and that with it the will always acts. But he insists that with it the will has the power not to act, and without it the will has the power to act, in the divided sense. On his view the will's power not to act or to act otherwise coexists with the predetermining influence, but the opposite act, or ceasing from the act, does not. Conversely, without that influence the power to act remains in the will, though without it that power is never brought into act.

From this he concludes that someone who omits an act that is commanded omits it freely and sins. Through sufficient help he could have kept the command; by God's mercy he could have had the motion needed to act; and by his own fault he prevented God from giving it to him.

source_text: XXVI. Sed multo major pars Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae sententiam istam hodie rejicit, & pertendit influxum illum praemoventem & praedeterminantem voluntates hominum ad singulos ipsorum actus, humani arbitrii libertatem prorsus evertere; ac praeterea inde sequi Deum esse peccati authorem, ut qui, ex ista sententia, homines praedeterminet etiam ad actus intrinsece malos, & quandam male agendi necessitatem iis imponat.
english: The great majority of the Roman Church's teachers, however, now reject this view. They argue that an influence premoving and predetermining human wills to each of their acts completely destroys the freedom of human choice.
They add that it would make God the author of sin, since on that view he predetermines people even to intrinsically evil acts and lays on them a kind of necessity to do wrong.

source_text: XXVII. Itaque longe aliter de concursu illo Dei philosophantur. Primo enim statuunt, Deum cum causis secundis concurrentem & cooperantem non aliquid agere, aut imprimere in ipsam facultatem quae agit, exempli gratia, in voluntatem nostram; sed tantum immediate influere & agere in ipsam actionem, & effectum causae secundae, eamque producere illo ipso momento quo producitur a causa secunda.
english: They therefore reason about God's concurrence quite differently. First, they hold that when God concurs and cooperates with secondary causes he does not do or impress anything on the faculty that acts, our will, for instance.
He only flows into and acts directly on the action itself and on the effect of the secondary cause, producing it at the very moment the secondary cause produces it.

source_text: XXVIII. Deinde consequenter docent actionem causae primae concurrentis cum causa secunda, non esse actionem reipsa diversam ab actione causae secundae, sed illam ipsam actionem, quatenus esse suum a causa prima accipit. Ita quum Deus, verbi causa, cum voluntate concurrit in volendi, vel nolendi actu, ipse non exerit, ex eorum mente, actionem aliquam in voluntatem, distinctam ab actione voluntatis ipsius; sed tantum esse confert actioni voluntatis simul cum voluntate, & actionem illam conservat. Ac proinde divina hac in parte cooperatio non est aliquid diversum a volitione nostra, sed ipsa nostra volitio, quatenus a Deo immediate pendet quoad sui productionem & conservationem.
english: Next, and consistently with this, they teach that the action of the first cause concurring with the secondary cause is not an action really distinct from that of the secondary cause. It is that same action, considered as receiving its being from the first cause.

So when God concurs with the will in an act of willing or refusing, he does not, on their view, exert on the will an action distinct from the will's own. He only gives being to the will's action together with the will, and keeps that action in being. God's cooperation here is therefore not something other than our act of will; it is our act of will itself, insofar as its production and preservation depend directly on God.

source_text: XXIX. Praeterea, quod etiam manifeste sequitur ex dictis, negant causam secundam a causa prima ad agendum moveri, aut ab eadem in agendo ad talem actionem edendam determinari. Adeoque, juxta eorum sententiam, causa secunda, & proinde voluntas, non ideo operatur quia Deus illam movet, & applicat ad agendum: sed potius Deus illi cooperatur, quia ipsa sese ad agendum disponit. Concursus autem & influxus divinus est aliquid ex se indifferens, quod a causis secundis ad varias actionum species determinatur.
english: They also deny, as plainly follows from the foregoing, that the first cause moves the secondary cause to act or determines it, in acting, to produce a given action.

On their view, then, the secondary cause, and so the will, does not act because God moves it and applies it to act; rather, God cooperates with it because it sets itself to act. God's concurrence and influence is of itself indifferent, and it is the secondary causes that determine it to the various kinds of action.

source_text: XXX. Haec & plura ejusdem generis prolixius diducta & exposita videre est apud Ludovicum Molinam in Concordia Liberi Arbitrii cum gratiae donis, &c. quaest. 14. disputat. 26. Ubi affirmat primo Deum ita cum causis secundis concurrere ad earum operationes & effectus, ut quemadmodum causa secunda immediate elicit suam operationem, & per eam terminum, seu effectum producit; sic Deus concursu quodam generali immediate influat cum ea in eandem operationem, & per operationem, seu actionem terminum illius, seu effectum producat. Secundo, Deum, quando concurrit cum causis secundis, influere ut causam universalem, influxu quodam indifferenti ad varias actiones & effectus, determinari vero influxum illum generalem ad diversas species actionum & effectuum a particulari influxu causarum secundarum, qui pro diversitate virtutis cujusque ad agendum diversus est. Non secus ac influxus solis, qui etiam universalis est, determinatur ab influxu hominis, ut producatur homo; & ab influxu equi, ut oriatur equus. Quod si causa libera sit, in ipsius potestate esse ita influere, ut producatur potius haec actio quam illa, puta velle, quam nolle, aut ambulare, quam sedere, & hic effectus potius quam ille, nempe hoc artefactum, potius quam aliud; Vel etiam suspendere omnino influxum, ne ulla sit actio. Tertio, ad nullius effectus productionem satis esse influxum Dei per concursum universalem, sine influxu causae secundae particularis a qua determinatur, neque vicissim influxum causae particularis, sine influxu Dei per concursum universalem, quo adjuvetur, & quem de lege ordinaria statuit nunquam denegare. Hos vero duos influxus mutuo ab invicem pendere, ut in rerum natura existant: imo non esse duas actiones, sed unam numero actionem, quae ut est a Deo illo modo influente, dicitur concursus generalis; ut vero a causa secunda, puta ab igne calefaciente, dicitur concursus, seu influxus ignis. Neque actionem illam habere quod sit hujus speciei, nempe calefactio, potius quam frigefactio, quia est a Deo per concursum universalem, sed quia est ab igne cum Deo cooperante per suam particularem virtutem.
english: These points, and more of the same kind, are worked out and explained at greater length by Luis de Molina in his Concordia of free choice with the gifts of grace, question 14, disputation 26.

He states, first, that God concurs with secondary causes in their operations and effects in this way: just as the secondary cause directly produces its operation and through it brings about its result or effect, so God, by a general concurrence, flows directly together with it into that same operation and through the operation or action brings about its result or effect.

Second, when God concurs with secondary causes he acts as a universal cause, by an influence indifferent to various actions and effects, and that general influence is determined to different kinds of action and effect by the particular influence of secondary causes, which differs according to the different power each has to act. The sun's influence, which is likewise universal, is determined by a man's influence to produce a man and by a horse's influence to produce a horse. If the cause is free, it is in its power to exert its influence so that this action rather than that results, say willing rather than refusing, or walking rather than sitting, and this effect rather than that, this artefact rather than another. Or it can withhold its influence altogether, so that there is no action at all.

Third, God's influence through universal concurrence is not enough to produce any effect without the influence of the particular secondary cause that determines it. Nor, conversely, is the particular cause's influence enough without God's influence through universal concurrence, which helps it and which by ordinary law God has resolved never to withhold. These two influences depend on each other in order to exist in reality; indeed they are not two actions but numerically one action. As it comes from God acting in that way it is called general concurrence; as it comes from the secondary cause, say from fire heating something, it is called the concurrence or influence of the fire. And that action is of this kind, heating rather than cooling, not because it comes from God through universal concurrence but because it comes from the fire, with God cooperating, through the fire's particular power.
